title_en: 'I'm the Albatross of Video Games' – Guillermo del Toro on Blade 2, Working With Kojima, and Lots of Red Bull
summary_en: We got the chance to sit down with the one and only Guillermo del Toro as part of our IGN30 Icons Series, where he let us in on his favorite games, how he made his iconic movies, and his experience working with some of the biggest stars in filmmaking.
body_en:
We got the chance to sit down with the one and only Guillermo del Toro as part of our IGN30 Icons Series, where he let us in on his favorite games, how he made his iconic movies, and his experience working with some of the biggest stars in filmmaking.
He also chatted about Pan’s Labyrinth , which is turning 20 years old this year. To celebrate, it’s coming back to theaters this weekend — but if you’d like some extra context before you sit down to see it again, check out our conversation with del Toro, who told us about the inspiration behind the Pale Man and how he stretched the movie’s budget to create some of its massive set pieces.
We’ve transcribed the interview in full below, where del Toro explained what it was like working with Wesley Snipes on Blade 2 and how he almost made a BioShock movie.
Brian Altano (IGN): From Kronos to The Shape of Water to Frankenstein, it is an honor to be talking to the maestro of movie monsters, Mr. Guillermo Del Toro. It's very nice to meet you. Thank you for coming. This is the 20th anniversary of Pan's Labyrinth, which makes me feel old. I don't know how you feel about it.
Guillermo del Toro: Older.
Brian Altano (IGN): So, you have been making crazy monsters in beautiful worlds for the longest time. You started off inspired by things like Universal’s monsters, [like the] Creature from the Black Lagoon. What is it about that era that spoke to you then, and continues to resonate with you now?
Guillermo del Toro: I think I was a monster kid, which means that the creatures are important in the storytelling of these fairytales, because I think they're fables or parables or fairytales. And it has to be creature-centric for me to be attracted to it. Everybody says, "Oh, don't show the creature." I think, show it, please. I'm seven years old. I want to see it. I want to love it. I want to see how well designed it is. I want to discover the whole world that comes in with the creature design. Creature design ushers a different reality. So those are important. When Milicent Patrick — who designed the Gill-man for Creature from the Black Lagoon — designed the Metaluna Mutant on Island Earth, when they gave her an opportunity, it came from outer space. She designed the creature. She has a signature, and I can see what her design signature is. And as a kid, it's like meeting a movie star. You say, "Oh, this was Jack Pierce designing this creature. This was Dick Smith. This was the Wesmers. This was all the makeup heroes of mine."
Brian Altano (IGN): So when you saw the sort of less tangible horror, which it's like a fog or a mist or something like that, you're like, "That's cool, but I want a monster.”
Guillermo del Toro: Well, that's what I want to make. That doesn't define what I want to watch. I want to watch everything that is good. But as a filmmaker, up until Frankenstein, I'm very creature-centric. I think that has changed now. I don't know what I am or where I'm going. I have sort of a new horizon, but Frankenstein was a culmination of my creature-centric period, which is, by the way, where is it rooted at? Little Red Ridinghood. You need the wolf. The wolf is the creature in that. And you need something that embodies a concept. Good, evil, purity, tragedy. The Creature in Frankenstein is a tragic humanity. Pan is a trickster. The Pale Man is a blind veracity. It's not just that they are cool-looking. It's that they embody the conceptual part of the tale. They actually mean something tangible. Godzilla is absolutely a first large-scale God, the power of nature, the tragedy of atomic energy. It's a concept made flesh.
Brian Altano (IGN): It's not just this wrecking ball that comes in. There's a pain behind it.
Guillermo del Toro: There is the tragic undertones of the design of Godzilla, the fact that they wanted the skin of Godzilla to look like the after effect of a nuclear blast victim. I mean, there is thought on that — the fact that he was this sort of grayish-brown in the original. There is a lot of thought. Jack Pierce designing the Grizzly on Frankenstein — he wanted to sort of retrofit the history of the autopsic work that put it together. The scars, the opening of the skull in a sort of weird, can-of-tomatoes way.
Brian Altano (IGN): You like to get your hands dirty. You like to build stuff. You make model kits. Your Cabinet of Curiosity is a very tangible thing. It feels like a lot of filmmakers are sort of moving around
or away from that, but that is something that feels so core to your philosophy of filmmaking.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. Each filmmaker is like, I see Chris Nolan completely going to battle for negative and he's entrenched there. I see Jim Cameron exploring beyond capture. He's actually melding actors’ performances with how it translates into digital. Each filmmaker is on a quest, I think. And my quest is handmade by humans for humans.
Brian Altano (IGN): I love that. Christopher Nolan mentioned that you were a big inspiration for a lot of his practical effects in the Odyssey, specifically the Cyclops.
Guillermo del Toro: Cyclops, yeah.
Brian Altano (IGN): Did you see it?
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, yeah. No, I saw it with him.
Brian Altano (IGN): Oh my God, that's awesome.
Guillermo del Toro: He said, "I want to show you the movie." And we saw it in IMAX. We talked after, we talked before. I mean, I think he's just — there is such a signature and such a vision. I mean, the word visionary is thrown around a little too much, but I think Chris has always been. I've known him now fortunately for about 15 years or more. And he's always been absolutely laser-focused.
Brian Altano (IGN): Did you like what he did with the cyclops?
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, I loved it.
Brian Altano (IGN): Me too.
Guillermo del Toro: Loved it. I mean, I love everything. I asked him, “So when Matt Damon is in the tempestuous waters, how did you do it?” He's like, "We put him in the water on a tempestuous day." It was so fantastic to hear him answer that. And I remember when I talked to him about his philosophy of sound mixing, because I asked him that back in the days of Interstellar, and he said, "To me, dialogue is part of the score. It's not so much what they say, but the rhythm of how they say it and the intention." And I thought that was… Now and then, when I mix, now and then I go, "It's a rhythmic thing."
Brian Altano (IGN): You worked on Mimic, which, for me, that was sort of like a Creature from the Black Lagoon for me. It's funny to say, right? Because when I was a kid and I did the same thing, I was going —
Guillermo del Toro: It's a monster movie.
Brian Altano (IGN): I was like, "I want to watch a monster movie." And I saw that one and the setting. I had grown up going to the Museum of Natural History in New York City.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. Well, that's where we went!
Brian Altano (IGN): And it actually changed that museum for me for a while, because I would go there and I'd be like, "Are we good?" All the rooms were a little dark.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, of course. The Natural History Museum in New York, to me, is Disneyland. It's a portal to imagination. And the exhibits are so exquisitely crafted. They are one of the places that have inspired me the most.
Brian Altano (IGN): I could spend hours looking up at that whale up there. The way that movie came together was sort of out of your hands. There were a lot of people kind of hacking it apart. Was there any time during that where you're like, "I don't want to do this anymore. This process is so..."
Guillermo del Toro: To a point. It's too early to quit when you're 33. That's true. You don't want to quit, but I wanted to quit that way of making movies. I was very careful to try to regain independence with Devil's Wagon supported by Pedro Almodovar. I was lucky enough that he liked what I did. And I made it a point. I was being pushed to do Blade 2 first. I said, "I'm doing Devil's Wagon first. I'm not going to go back to an industrial movie making environment until I cleanse my soul." And I made it a point. Many times people say, "Oh, I would never sell out." Well, you don't know until someone's buying. And I can tell you 100% sure of the many defects I have. I've never sold out.
Brian Altano (IGN): I believe it. I believe it. Do you think that you had to go through what you did with Mimic before you did Blade 2 and Hellboy?
Guillermo del Toro: Yes, because it makes a difference. I said, “Okay, so when I do Blade 2, I'm not going to try to fashion an auteurial [film].” I'm going to just go and say, “Okay, can I give you a six pack pizza, vox, balls-to-the-wall, fun, almost like a musical, and have it ooze atmosphere and coolness. And then you don't have to worry about anything else. Still, there's streaks of Frankenstein on it.
Brian Altano (IGN): Again, you've mentioned before the thing about sort of filmmakers making one movie. Can you explain that philosophy a bit?
Guillermo del Toro: It's actually, ‘One life fuels a movie.’ I would argue that the range would be between Devil's Wagon and Pacific Rim. That's the range of the modulation of the thing. But at the end of the day, you have a style, you have a signature. And I find it amazing with, for example, Alfonso Cuarón. You can do Gravity or you can do Roma. You would say it's not the same movie, but it is. Because I know what Alfonso's looking for, which is the connection with reality of the earth, almost like a transcendental approach. Gravity. I remember I was in the middle of the post-production, the studio didn't believe in the movie, and they wanted Alfonso to put helicopters coming to the rescue of Sandra Bullock at the end. I said, "No." He said, "Well, what about the sound of helicopters?" "No.” "What about the radio saying, ‘We're coming for you?’” I said, "No.” He said, "The only thing that she's recuperating is her footing on earth. That's what the movie's about.” Because it grounds it. It's an auteurial movie. So you have a voice and you use it for different songs, but it's the same voice.
Brian Altano (IGN): When you made Blade 2, you can just tell you had a ton of fun making that movie.
Guillermo del Toro: Actually, it's probably that and Pacific Rim are the two most fun movies I've ever shot. I really had fun. It may have been held by the fact that Red Bull had just come out and I didn't know how to use it. So I was drinking, and I'm not joking, about 40 Red Bulls a day.
Brian Altano (IGN): Man,that is amazing.
Guillermo del Toro: I was like in a cocaine movie. I was like, come on, let's go. And I would order cases and cases of Red Bull and throw them to the extras.
Brian Altano (IGN): I want to change the IGN review scale now. Instead of one to 10, I want to be like, “This is a 40 Red Bull movie.”
Guillermo del Toro: When I went back to America, Red Bull started traveling from Europe to there. And my doctor said, "You cannot consume more than four." I was drinking 40. The arterial damage, man.
Brian Altano (IGN): They announced a Blade reboot at Comic-Con years ago and they were never able to make it. And why do you think it's so difficult to get a movie like that done?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm telling you, and I mean it because I know it, 50% of the bladeness of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
Brian Altano (IGN): Wesley Snipes?
Guillermo del Toro: 100%. He is not the most linear actor to deal with, right?
Brian Altano (IGN): Right.
Guillermo del Toro: But every time he stood in front of the lens, I said, “That’s a movie star. That’s Blade.” Completely. For example, I showed him a gun we designed — beautiful, [Dieter] Reinhardt, Ron Pearlman ends up using it, with a blade on the front — and he looked at it. “Not for Blade. Cold gun, but not for Blade.” I said, “Why?” He said, “Because Blade is the weapon.” He said, “I don't want the toys. I want the man. The man is a dangerous guy. You give me too many toys, and that’s the Batmobile and the Bat belt. That's not Blade.” And I went, “Ah, this guy knows it.” And Every time [Snipes] landed, every time he turned, he’s a Neil Adams comic book [character]. And he has the natural sort of comic book [look]. I think Blade 1, Steve’s movie, changed the history of comic book movies for me, period. Because before that, you had either the cleanliness, the beauty, and sort of wholesomeness of Richard Donner's Superman, or you had the quirkiness of Tim Burton’s Batman. But this is what ushered the ‘tude, the edge. Without Steve Norrington's Blade, I don't think there is The Matrix. I don't think there is X-Men. I think what they did is monumental. And then I inherited and was completely, irresponsibly happy to do that.”
Brian Altano (IGN): So 50% of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
Guillermo del Toro: 100%. 100% is 50%.
Brian Altano (IGN): And the other 50% is Red Bull.
Guillermo del Toro: The other 50% is the filmmaker articulating. I mean, I had four or five moving boxes worth of dailies from [Stephen Norrington's] movie. And I studied all those VHS tapes. I understood exactly how he shot it. He did some formations that were really, extraordinarily weird. For example, he had a low camera with a longer lens in front of a high camera with a wide lens facing each other. His assistant called it — very impolitely and politically [incorrect] — they called it the Polish firing squad position. I didn't make that joke. I just repeated it. And then I started his formations and I said, “Okay, I'm going to go at it differently.” But there is one setup on Blade 2, which is 13 cameras working at the same time like a ballet. This camera is moving this way and then it crosses this one right on time for my cut. So I would cut before we shoot. So what they did is extraordinary. I know it.
Brian Altano (IGN): In your Blade 2 movie commentary, there's a sequence where you say, "This is my Dr. Manhattan shot." I love that so much. Obviously as a Watchman fan, a lot of directors sort of hide their influences.
Guillermo del Toro: I talk about them.
Brian Altano (IGN): Explain that, because obviously some people, I think they're sort of a little ashamed of jumping off of an idea that they may have seen before, that they might have inherited. But you've always been —
Guillermo del Toro: Because you're not rephrasing. When you take something and change it, it's a permutation. I mean, for example, the classical compositions are only so many. When you're doing a format, for example, you're doing a tango. It has to be a tango. It's on a certain tempo. When you're doing a waltz, there is a tempo. So you're taking a form and you're completely remixing it. Every chef in every restaurant, in every part of the world, whether it's a fast food service or… the hot cuisine of Michelin star restaurants, they're using the same ingredients. And you're not ashamed of pepper. You're not ashamed of a carrot, or what they call the mother sauce in France in the cooking — You have celery, carrot, onion. Ingredients are ingredients. And when I say, “This is my Dr. Manhattan shot,” well, I'm saying it's my Jack Kirby shot. Because that shot is very Jack Kirby. And then Jack Kirby, you have to talk to him to [see] where it comes from, but you are probably influenced by Milton Caniff. It's a lineage of storytellers. There is not such a thing as an ingredient you should not mention, because as we were discussing, I think for chefs coming up, it's important to disclose how you cook, how you bleach, how you blanch the potatoes. It's good to say this is what I did and it's very different.
Brian Altano (IGN): I appreciate that because I think that the making of stuff, the behind the scenes stuff, it is exactly the kind of thing that inspires new filmmakers.
Guillermo del Toro: Yes, 100%.
Brian Altano (IGN): And you made The Making of Frankenstein, which I watched immediately after Frankenstein. And it was fascinating to me, because I think coming from an era where you grew up looking at magazines of like, this is how they're making movies or watching the DVD actuals and Blu-rays and stuff like that, that's the stuff that people see and they go, "This isn't impossible anymore. This is something that I can start doing myself."
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. I mean, as of lately, the last few releases on Blu-ray, I paid for the totality, or most of the behind the scenes content, because I wanted it to be in the disc. And I don't want it to be in the disc to sing our praises — I want it, because if you live in a part of the world or in an economic condition where you cannot afford film school, but your local library has the discs, you can learn how to make movies. If you come at it sincerely, it's not from the beginning. You want to talk about how hard it was and how you were thinking [about] this thing, but you went that way. So, I think they're very useful sort of substitutes for film school.
Brian Altano (IGN): Is there sort of like a scene in the movies you've made where every artist knows how difficult it is to translate the idea that's in your head to something that exists finally in real life, whether that's a drawing or a painting. It always filters and changes in some way. Is there a specific scene or collection of scenes that has come the closest from being like, "This is the idea in my mind. This is the scene in the film."
Guillermo del Toro: The Pale Man.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yeah?
Guillermo del Toro: The Pale Man in Pan’s Labyrinth. It changed a lot, but once the creature was set, once I found the creature in pre-production, I looked at a photo of a manta ray face up. And I saw the poster of Phantasm where the woman is screaming and you can see her eyes. And through many permutations, it ended up being that creature. But the moment I saw that creature, the scene was exactly what it is. And Pacific Rim, I knew exactly what I wanted to do to give the scale to the robots. I knew I wanted them in the rain. I knew I wanted them in what I call Goth-tech. And finally, I would say Frankenstein. But Frankenstein changed a lot when Jacob Elordi came in. So I mean, to some degree, those would be very close.
Brian Altano (IGN): Because at a certain point it is out of your hands, especially when it becomes part of an actor's experience.
Guillermo del Toro: It's never quite that simple. People think filmmaking is chess. It isn't. It's a contact sport. Or you're playing tennis. They serve, you return. Directing is knowing how to serve, but you also know how to return. If you think it's all about control, then this is a problem. People think that filmmaking is like multitask prompting, like AI. “Oh, I want this.” No, you're really building. It's a very, very dirty, non-linear business. And that's why one of the many reasons I'm against generative AI, is because it'll get you to mediocrity really quick. It'll get you to the middle really quick. And that may be an image. It's not film. It's not cinema.
Brian Altano (IGN): I think it's a very cynical approach to creating stuff where you only want the results and not the process. And the process is the fun part.
Guillermo del Toro: Let me put it this way: I can tell you, “Look, I'm faster than Usain Bolt.” I said, "Really?" I go, "Yeah, in my car." "Okay, well then, you're not a runner. You're in a car. It's not a f**king sport. That's not art. You're in a car."
Brian Altano (IGN): I think that's my favorite thing anyone has ever said about AI.
Guillermo del Toro: And you're in a f**king Volvo.
Brian Altano (IGN): Thank you so much for that. I'm very much against generative AI, and that is the best way it could possibly be put.
Guillermo del Toro: Look, the risk is this. Every single bad idea in the history of totalitarianism comes involved in a concept that sounds reasonably beneficial. The mother, the motherland — sounds really nice. Democratization of the arts. It's not that. They want your money. They want you to buy their app. They don't care about that. The discourse between the soul of mankind and the arts is a very sacred discourse. It's very intimate. It's molecularly important to stay human. Please, please. Don't give me an app. Please.
Brian Altano (IGN): I will not. Your unmade filmography is legendary.
Guillermo del Toro: Yes.
Brian Altano (IGN): Somewhere it exists in your brain. How do those sort of stories, those movies, live on? Do you ever go back through your sketchbooks? Can you watch them in your mind?
Guillermo del Toro: No. They're in the sketchbooks, and sometimes I repurpose ideas. For example, the wings of the Angel of Death came from a project that I was writing in ‘98. Partially, the Pale Man came from a sketch I did in ‘99. So you repurpose. Your diaries with drawings become a sort of catalog and you go through them and go, "Oh, I've never done that. Let me do it now." There's a sketch for a thing that I designed for Pan’s Labyrinth that is coming out in a stop motion movie I'm doing now.
Brian Altano (IGN): That’s awesome. I love that. So, you find a way to reincorporate these old ideas even if —
Guillermo del Toro: Well, it's a dialogue with yourself.
Brian Altano (IGN): Yeah.
Guillermo del Toro: You're talking to the time when you were a very different person. So you reactivate yourself.
Brian Altano (IGN): We talked about Pan's Labyrinth turning 20 this year. This was definitely the first movie that kind of broke over the crust of the usual people that were coming to your movies. All of a sudden, you had film critics and stuff like that [who] were really paying attention to you. Did that change you, having these new sets of eyes on you?
Guillermo del Toro: Well, Chronos and Devil's Backbone had that, but they had it in a very, very arthouse niche. What Pan's Labyrinth did is, the first movie that I willed to do my way with a slightly larger scale — The Shape of Water. And Pan’s Labyrinth cost exactly the same, $19.3 million, both movies. And [I looked] at the scale. And I said, "I'm going to will..." Alejandro González Iñárritu one day said to me, because I said, "How the hell

Brian Altano (IGN): I was like, "I want to watch a monster movie." And I saw that one and the setting. I had grown up going to the Museum of Natural History in New York City.
Guillermo del Toro: Yeah. Well, that's where we went!
Brian Altano (IGN): And it actually changed that museum for me for a while, because I would go there and I'd be like, "Are we good?" All the rooms were a little dark.

Guillermo del Toro: Yeah, of course. The Natural History Museum in New York, to me, is Disneyland. It's a portal to imagination. And the exhibits are so exquisitely crafted. They are one of the places that have inspired me the most.

Brian Altano (IGN): Again, you've mentioned before the thing about sort of filmmakers making one movie. Can you explain that philosophy a bit?

Guillermo del Toro: It's actually, ‘One life fuels a movie.’ I would argue that the range would be between Devil's Wagon and Pacific Rim. That's the range of the modulation of the thing. But at the end of the day, you have a style, you have a signature. And I find it amazing with, for example, Alfonso Cuarón. You can do Gravity or you can do Roma. You would say it's not the same movie, but it is. Because I know what Alfonso's looking for, which is the connection with reality of the earth, almost like a transcendental approach. Gravity. "No.” "What about the radio saying, ‘We're coming for you?’” I said, "No.” He said, "The only thing that she's recuperating is her footing on earth. Brian Altano (IGN): They announced a Blade reboot at Comic-Con years ago and they were never able to make it. And why do you think it's so difficult to get a movie like that done?
Guillermo del Toro: I'm telling you, and I mean it because I know it, 50% of the bladeness of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
Guillermo del Toro: 100%. He is not the most linear actor to deal with, right?

Guillermo del Toro: But every time he stood in front of the lens, I said, “That’s a movie star. That’s Blade.” Completely. For example, I showed him a gun we designed — beautiful, [Dieter] Reinhardt, Ron Pearlman ends up using it, with a blade on the front — and he looked at it. “Not for Blade. Cold gun, but not for Blade.” I said, “Why?” He said, “Because Blade is the weapon.” He said, “I don't want the toys. I want the man. The man is a dangerous guy. You give me too many toys, and that’s the Batmobile and the Bat belt. That's not Blade.” And I went, “Ah, this guy knows it.” And Every time [Snipes] landed, every time he turned, he’s a Neil Adams comic book [character]. And he has the natural sort of comic book [look]. I think Blade 1, Steve’s movie, changed the history of comic book movies for me, period. Because before that, you had either the cleanliness, the beauty, and sort of wholesomeness of Richard Donner's Superman, or you had the quirkiness of Tim Burton’s Batman. But this is what ushered the ‘tude, the edge. Without Steve Norrington's Blade, I don't think there is The Matrix. I don't think there is X-Men. I think what they did is monumental. And then I inherited and was completely, irresponsibly happy to do that.”
Brian Altano (IGN): So 50% of Blade is Wesley Snipes.
